bio.en: Annie Pearl is Chief Product Officer at Calendly, previously CPO at Glassdoor and a product director at Fox, with experience across consumer and B2B product.
bio.zh: Annie Pearl 是 Calendly 首席产品官，此前曾任 Glassdoor 首席产品官及 Fox 产品总监，在消费级与 B2B 产品方面均有丰富经验。

summary.en: Annie defines strategy as an integrated set of choices about where you'll play and how you'll win, anchored in a clear winning aspiration. She walks through how Calendly builds product and grew—including the wild story of its first 1,000 users—and how it built a sales team atop a product-led growth motion. The conversation also shares advice on getting into product management and a few killer tips for using Calendly itself.
summary.zh: Annie 将战略定义为一组关于“在哪里竞争、如何取胜”的连贯选择，锚定在清晰的取胜愿望上。她讲述了 Calendly 如何做产品、如何增长（包括获得前 1000 名用户的传奇故事），以及如何在产品驱动增长的基础上建立起销售团队。对话还分享了进入产品管理行业的建议，以及几个使用 Calendly 的绝妙技巧。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Strategy is really just an integrated set of choices that outline how you're going to win in whatever marketplace you choose. And so, a good product strategy is going to answer questions like what's your winning aspiration? But maybe more importantly, where are you going to play? What are the markets you're going to go after? What are the segments of those markets? What are the personas in the segments of those markets? And then, how are you going to win with a target audience?
turns.zh: 策略实际上只是一组综合的选择，概述了您将如何在您选择的任何市场中获胜。因此，良好的产品策略将回答诸如您的制胜愿望是什么？但也许更重要的是，你要去哪里玩？您要关注哪些市场？这些市场有哪些细分市场？这些市场细分中的人物角色是什么？然后，你将如何赢得目标受众？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: All right, well I love this question to kick us off. We actually have a whole blog post about this if you're curious to learn more.
turns.zh: 好吧，我喜欢用这个问题来开始我们的讨论。如果您想了解更多信息，我们实际上有一篇关于此的完整博客文章。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, okay.
turns.zh: 哦好的。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: But I think that at a high level, I think I recommend first really just kind of opening the door for the person you're trying to schedule time with to share their availability first. So instead of just sending the link, I usually start the email with something like looking forward to connecting, feel free to share, sometimes you're available or if easier, you can choose to find time on my calendar using the Calendly link here. So, opening the door to let them choose before you offer up your Calendly link, I think is a little bit of a subtle way to let them take the lead if they want. (00:05:08): And the second piece I would recommend too is once you opened that door, you can further reduce the effort on the recipient by adding times you're available directly in the email. So, when you go to share a Calendly link, there's an option to add times to email and you can then just paste those directly into the email you're creating, so that reduces yet another sort of point of friction to ask the user to click the link and get taken to Calendly. So, opening the door and then adding times to email are two things that I do to really make sure that it's not awkward and it doesn't put the burden on the other person.
turns.zh: 但我认为，在较高的层面上，我认为我建议首先为您想要安排时间的人打开大门，以便首先分享他们的空闲时间。因此，我通常不会只发送链接，而是以诸如期待连接、随意分享、有时您有空或者如果更容易的话，您可以选择使用此处的 Calendly 链接在我的日历上查找时间之类的内容开始电子邮件。因此，在你提供 Calendly 链接之前打开大门让他们选择，我认为这是一种微妙的方式，可以让他们在愿意的情况下发挥主导作用。 (00:05:08)：我也推荐的第二件事是，一旦您打开那扇门，您可以通过直接在电子邮件中添加您的可用时间来进一步减少收件人的工作量。因此，当您分享 Calendly 链接时，可以选择向电子邮件添加时间，然后您可以将这些时间直接粘贴到您正在创建的电子邮件中，这样就减少了要求用户单击链接并进入 Calendly 的另一种摩擦点。因此，打开门然后添加电子邮件时间是我做的两件事，以真正确保这不会尴尬，并且不会给其他人带来负担。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Transitioning a little bit to product, the main focus of chat, you transitioned into product from being a lawyer. You told me at one point that a lot of people ask you for advice about how to transition into product from other functions, especially non-technical functions as someone without a technical background. So, what advice do you give people when they ask you how to transition into a product role?
turns.zh: 稍微过渡到产品，聊天的主要焦点，你从律师过渡到产品。您曾经告诉我，很多人向您询问如何从其他功能（尤其是没有技术背景的人的非技术功能）过渡到产品。那么，当人们问你如何过渡到产品角色时，你会给他们什么建议呢？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: I got what I'll call lucky, which is I kind of stumbled into product management after law school, joined the founding team of a startup and ended up doing product management there. But when I think about folks who are looking to get in their product management, I think there's really two paths. I think one is more formal in nature. There are associate product manager programs out there and many scaled companies, Google, Meta. All have APM programs that you can formally apply to. And actually, when we were at Box, much earlier stage company than either of those companies I just mentioned, we actually created an APM program to help grow our bench of more junior PM. So, I think you can actually find APM programs even at smaller, earlier stage companies than even kind of big tech. So that's one, it's just formal APM programs. (00:07:07): I think another "more formal" way to get into PM is really by just directly applying to a junior PM role where there's no expectation of any sort of experience. I've usually seen this work best when you're already working somewhere in some product adjacency. Maybe you're in customer support, implementation, or maybe you're a sales engineer. But you can look at the internal job board and find junior PM roles that are posted and that's one way to make the move. So that's kind of on the formal side like APM programs and just applying via internal job boards. (00:07:38): I think on the informal side, really two suggestions here. The first one is to seek out opportunities to shadow or partner closely with a product manager and maybe even offer to take on some work. So, some of the best PMs that I've brought over to product from other functions, they really start by expressing interest in product and then start partnering closely with the product manager and maybe even doing a little bit of product work before they make that transition. (00:08:02): And one tactical suggestion is there's oftentimes companies will have subject matter expert programs where they want to pair someone from a go-to-market function with a certain product squad or a certain product area. And so that's becoming a SME. It allows you to really get more involved and embedded into the product team. So, that's one suggestion. And then maybe last one is just the path I did, which is joining an early stage startup. There's really usually an expectation that everyone's going to get their hands dirty doing a lot of different things. And so, I think that's one way where you might have an opportunity to try product management if you end up joining an early stage company.
turns.zh: 我得到了我所说的幸运，那就是我在法学院毕业后偶然进入了产品管理领域，加入了一家初创公司的创始团队，并最终在那里从事产品管理。但当我想到那些想要进入产品管理领域的人时，我认为实际上有两条路。我认为一种本质上更正式。那里有副产品经理计划，还有许多规模化的公司，比如谷歌、Meta。所有项目都有您可以正式申请的 APM 计划。事实上，当我们在 Box（比我刚才提到的任何一家公司都早得多的公司）工作时，我们实际上创建了一个 APM 计划来帮助培养我们的初级 PM 人员。因此，我认为，即使在规模较小、处于早期阶段的公司中，实际上也可以找到 APM 项目，甚至比大型科技公司还要多。这就是其中之一，它只是正式的 APM 计划。 (00:07:07)：我认为进入 PM 的另一种“更正式”方式实际上是直接申请初级 PM 职位，不需要任何经验。我通常认为，当您已经在某些产品邻近的某个地方工作时，这种方法效果最好。也许您从事客户支持、实施工作，或者您是销售工程师。但你可以查看内部招聘委员会并找到已发布的初级 PM 职位，这是采取行动的一种方法。因此，这属于正式方面，例如 APM 计划，只是通过内部招聘委员会进行申请。 (00:07:38)：我认为在非正式方面，这里确实有两个建议。第一个是寻找机会跟随产品经理或与产品经理密切合作，甚至可能主动承担一些工作。因此，我从其他职能部门调到产品部门的一些最好的产品经理，他们实际上是从表达对产品的兴趣开始的，然后开始与产品经理密切合作，甚至可能在进行过渡之前做一些产品工作。 (00:08:02)：一个战术建议是，公司通常会有主题专家计划，他们希望将市场推广职能部门的人员与特定产品团队或特定产品领域配对。因此，这正在成为中小企业。它可以让您真正更多地参与并融入产品团队。所以，这是一个建议。也许最后一条就是我所做的，那就是加入一家早期初创公司。人们通常期望每个人都会亲自去做很多不同的事情。因此，我认为如果您最终加入一家早期公司，这可能是您有机会尝试产品管理的一种方式。

And so, they make that really well known and they're even willing to do some work on the side to help out and really show and demonstrate the skills before they have the job. So, I've seen that one to actually probably bring the most folks over in my role in terms of being on the product leadership side.
turns.zh: 是的，我在内部带了很多人来寻找对产品真正感兴趣的人，他们表达了他们的兴趣，他们想要帮助，他们想要学习，他们渴望，他们好奇。因此，他们让这一点众所周知，他们甚至愿意在获得这份工作之前做一些兼职工作来帮助并真正展示和展示技能。因此，我发现，在产品领导方面，实际上可能会吸引最多的人来担任我的角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On the APM program route, are there any APM programs you recommend? Because I'm sure people hear this and they're like, "Yeah, but I don't know where to apply. I don't know which ones are good." I don't know if you have a list, but just what comes to mind as APM programs to go pursue?
turns.zh: 在APM课程路线上，有哪些值得推荐的APM课程吗？因为我确信人们听到这个后会想，“是的，但我不知道去哪里申请。我不知道哪些是好的。”我不知道您是否有一个清单，但是作为 APM 计划，您会想到什么？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: The folks who started it all was Google, with the Google APM program. And Meta obviously has a pretty strong robust APM program. But as I mentioned around Box, I think those are obviously very, very competitive and most people want to get into them. It may be better to try and find a company like Box or a company that's a bit earlier stage, not as scaled to think about looking at those APM programs. And I'm sure if you want to, go to glassdoor.com where I used to work at Glassdoor, so had to throw that in there. You could search for associate product manager and I think you'll find a whole host of open roles that you might be able to apply to.
turns.zh: 这一切的始作俑者是 Google，其推出了 Google APM 计划。 Meta 显然拥有相当强大的 APM 程序。但正如我在 Box 中提到的，我认为这些显然竞争非常非常激烈，大多数人都想加入其中。尝试找到像 Box 这样的公司或处于较早期阶段的公司可能会更好，而不是考虑查看那些 APM 程序的规模。我确信如果你愿意，可以访问 glassdoor.com，我曾经在 Glassdoor 工作过，所以不得不把它放在那里。您可以搜索副产品经理，我想您会找到大量您可以申请的空缺职位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a cool tip. I haven't heard of that. Go to Glassdoor and search for APM. So, you search for companies that have an APM title.
turns.zh: 这是一个很酷的提示。我没听说过。转到 Glassdoor 并搜索 APM。因此，您搜索具有 APM 称号的公司。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yes. You could just use associate product manager and you'll see all the open jobs out there and then go apply to them.
turns.zh: 是的。您可以只使用副产品经理，您会看到所有空缺职位，然后去申请它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's cool. Okay, good tip. What I find, and you mentioned this the best, if you have the option is internal transfer. If you're just like another function, you find someone that can help you move into the role.
turns.zh: 这很酷。好的，好提示。我发现，如果您可以选择内部转移，您提到的最好的就是内部转移。如果您只是喜欢另一个职能，您会找到可以帮助您进入该职位的人。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: You have the relationships, you can show your work really well. The other thing I would say is when I think about folks who have successfully transferred over, I think they tend to have a couple of characteristics. They're usually very curious, they tend to be really passionate about the product and solving customer problems. And sometimes, they've even tinkered with a side project as a way to hone their PM skills. So, I think as you're thinking about making that transition, those types of characteristics really showing eagerness and interest in the product itself and solving customer problems are also great ways to get noticed and increase your chances.
turns.zh: 你有了关系，你就能很好地展示你的作品。我想说的另一件事是，当我想到那些成功转学的人时，我认为他们往往有几个特点。他们通常非常好奇，他们往往对产品和解决客户问题充满热情。有时，他们甚至会修改一个副业项目，作为磨练 PM 技能的一种方式。因此，我认为当您考虑进行这种转变时，那些真正表现出对产品本身的渴望和兴趣以及解决客户问题的特征也是获得关注并增加机会的好方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Why do you think it is that not more companies have an APM program? It feels like such a win for so many people. Why is it just so rare?
turns.zh: 您认为为什么没有更多的公司拥有 APM 计划？对于很多人来说，这感觉就像是一场胜利。为什么它如此罕见？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah, I think when we built this at Box, so drawing on that experience, it was a lot of work. If you're going to do it, you want to do it really well and you want to create an environment where you can help the associate product managers be successful, the goal is to ultimately graduate everyone from the APM program into being a product manager. And so, I think it takes a lot of intentionality and for us, it took a lot of work. We had to make sure we had clarity around the interview process. We had to make sure we had clarity around expectations in the role. We wanted to have a training element. (00:12:16): We wanted to make sure that, again, we're setting people up for success. So, I think companies have to be at a stage of scale where they can really invest and they have the excess capacity to build the program in a way. I think that's going to help make sure everyone who comes through it has a chance at really learning, growing and ultimately being successful.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为当我们在 Box 开发这个产品时，利用这些经验，我们做了很多工作。如果你要做这件事，你想做得很好，你想创造一个可以帮助副产品经理取得成功的环境，目标是最终让 APM 计划中的每个人都成为产品经理。因此，我认为这需要很大的意愿，对我们来说，这需要大量的工作。我们必须确保面试过程清晰。我们必须确保我们对这个角色的期望有明确的认识。我们想要有一个培训元素。 (00:12:16)：我们希望再次确保我们正在为人们的成功做好准备。因此，我认为公司必须处于可以真正投资的规模阶段，并且有足够的能力以某种方式构建该项目。我认为这将有助于确保每个经历过这一过程的人都有机会真正学习、成长并最终取得成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's the same thing we found at Airbnb. There's a PM that was so excited to make the APM program and it just never really happens. It just takes so much work. And to your point, you have to set up for success. You want to make sure there's clear paths and you upgrade to a regular PM and have the interview.
turns.zh: 我们在 Airbnb 也发现了同样的情况。有一位 PM 非常兴奋地制定了 APM 计划，但它从未真正发生过。这需要做很多工作。就您而言，您必须为成功做好准备。您需要确保有清晰的路径，然后升级为正式产品经理并接受面试。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: And are we doing, is this really an APM program for internal folks? Is this external? Are we going to be really trying to promote this? So, I think there's a lot of ancillary activities around the actual program itself that have to be taken into consideration to make sure that it is actually very successful.
turns.zh: 我们在做什么，这真的是一个针对内部人员的 APM 计划吗？这是外在的吗？我们真的要努力推广这一点吗？因此，我认为围绕实际计划本身有很多辅助活动必须考虑在内，以确保它实际上非常成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Maybe a last point we should probably imagine you agree with is generally just hard to get into product management. That's like the default. There's just not that many roles at companies versus say, engineers or some other functions.
turns.zh: 是的。也许我们应该想象您同意的最后一点通常很难进入产品管理领域。这就像默认的一样。与工程师或其他一些职能部门相比，公司中的角色并不多。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, I think that's just like there are not that many roles. It's a difficult role to break into, but these are the ways you can do it if you actually want to.
turns.zh: 所以，我认为这就像没有那么多角色一样。这是一个很难进入的角色，但如果你真的想的话，这些都是你可以做到的方法。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: That's right. Yep.
turns.zh: 这是正确的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So, I want to transition a little bit to talking about Calendly.
turns.zh: 好的。所以，我想稍微过渡一下 Calendly。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There are two areas I want to go. One is just how do you build product at Calendly? What have you learned about product development and team building? And then two, talk about how Calendly grows and what you've learned about growing a product like Calendly. It's such an interesting product, especially from a growth perspective. So, to start on just how product is built at Calendly, just a little context. How many product managers are there and how many PMs are there? How many people total, roughly? Yeah, just to give us a little bit of [inaudible 00:13:57].
turns.zh: 我想去的地方有两个。一是你如何在 Calendly 构建产品？您在产品开发和团队建设方面学到了什么？然后第二点，谈谈 Calendly 是如何发展的，以及您在发展 Calendly 这样的产品时学到了什么。这是一个非常有趣的产品，尤其是从增长的角度来看。因此，要开始了解 Calendly 的产品是如何构建的，只需了解一些背景信息。有多少个产品经理，有多少个PM？总共有多少人，大概？是的，只是为了给我们一点点 [听不清 00:13:57]。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Let's see, when I joined about two years ago, I think the company was about 150 people and I think we're about 600 now. And then the product team, there were about 15 product managers and designers when I joined again about two years ago, and I think we're around 60 this year.
turns.zh: 让我们看看，当我大约两年前加入时，我认为公司大约有 150 人，而现在我们大约有 600 人。然后是产品团队，大约两年前我再次加入时，大约有 15 名产品经理和设计师，我想今年我们大约有 60 名。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. So, 60 product managers.
turns.zh: 哇。那么，60名产品经理。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Product managers, designers, and a research team. Yeah.
turns.zh: 产品经理、设计师和研究团队。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. What about just PMs?
turns.zh: 知道了。如果只是 PM 呢？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: PMs probably, my guess is 20.
turns.zh: PM一下吧，我猜是20个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 凉爽的。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Twenty-ish. Yeah.
turns.zh: 二十岁左右。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And then, can you talk about how the product team is structured roughly? If you think about a tree, [inaudible 00:14:30] tree.
turns.zh: 凉爽的。那么，您能谈谈产品团队的大致架构吗？如果你想到一棵树，[听不清 00:14:30] 树。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah. So, as I mentioned, we've got product managers, we have designers, we have a research team, and then product operations. And then, on my product leadership team, we have head of design, head of research, head of product operations. And then, within the product management team, I have leaders across core, across enterprise and platform.
turns.zh: 是的。因此，正如我提到的，我们有产品经理、设计师、研究团队，然后是产品运营。然后，在我的产品领导团队中，我们有设计主管、研究主管、产品运营主管。然后，在产品管理团队中，我有跨核心、跨企业和平台的领导者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So, you manage the design team and engineering team, you said?
turns.zh: 知道了。那么，你说，你管理着设计团队和工程团队？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Not engineering. Design, product and research. Yeah.
turns.zh: 不是工程。设计、产品和研究。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Something that I find is one of the big differences between product orgs is design reporting up to a product leader versus not. What's the rationale there? And then has Calendly tried a different approach?
turns.zh: 知道了。我发现产品组织之间的最大区别之一是向产品负责人报告的设计与不向产品负责人报告的设计。这里面有什么道理吗？那么 Calendly 是否尝试过不同的方法？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah. So, when I was at Glassdoor in the CPO role, I had the opportunity to lead design for the first time. So, coming into Calendly, I had led both product and design as well as research. And so, I think it made sense given I'd already done it once to keep that structure coming into Calendly. I think at the end of the day, the real benefit of the structure is really to say at the end, we want to be thinking about everything we're doing through the lens of the end-to-end user experience. And so, if we have product managers who are really prioritizing the problems we're going to go after, and we've got designers who are really trying to think about how do we bring solutions to life to solve those problems, having both of those functions roll into one person just really allows us to think more holistically around the end-to-end user experience. (00:15:53): So, certainly, it can work where you have product and design reporting into different leaders that ultimately report into the CEO, but when you get to this level of scale from just a pure people management, but also just the scale of the business, you know often see this consolidation where product and design start to roll into one leader. And at least in my experience, I think it can help ensure that all the different pieces of work are integrated well together and ultimately deliver a better experience for customers.
turns.zh: 是的。因此，当我在 Glassdoor 担任首席产品官时，我第一次有机会领导设计。因此，进入 Calendly 后，我领导了产品、设计以及研究。因此，我认为这是有道理的，因为我已经做过一次以保持该结构进入 Calendly。我认为归根结底，该结构的真正好处实际上是在最后说，我们希望通过端到端用户体验的角度来思考我们所做的一切。因此，如果我们有真正优先考虑我们要解决的问题的产品经理，并且有真正尝试思考如何将解决方案付诸实践来解决这些问题的设计师，那么将这两个功能集中到一个人身上确实可以让我们更全面地思考端到端的用户体验。 (00:15:53)：所以，当然，如果你向不同的领导者报告产品和设计，最终向首席执行官汇报，那么它可以发挥作用，但是当你从纯粹的人员管理以及业务规模达到这种规模时，你知道经常会看到这种整合，即产品和设计开始向一个领导者滚动。至少根据我的经验，我认为这有助于确保所有不同的工作能够很好地集成在一起，并最终为客户提供更好的体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, it sounds like before you joined it wasn't like that. And if that's true, was there something that improved with that shift?
turns.zh: 所以，听起来你加入之前并不是这样的。如果这是真的，那么这种转变是否带来了一些改进？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: So, the structure was there that way. At that time, we didn't have a head of design, so we had a lot of really great individual contributors and who had been, many of whom had been with the company for quite some time and really contributed to the great user experience that existed in the product. But we didn't have a design leader. So, one of the first leadership hires I made was to bring in a head of design to really build out that function. And then, that head of design is a peer partnering with the different heads of products across the product management organization as well.
turns.zh: 所以，结构就是这样的。当时，我们没有设计主管，所以我们有很多非常出色的个人贡献者，其中许多人已经在公司工作了很长一段时间，并为产品中存在的出色用户体验做出了真正的贡献。但我们没有设计领导者。因此，我聘用的第一个领导层就是聘请一位设计主管来真正构建该功能。然后，该设计主管也是与产品管理组织中不同产品主管合作的同事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What about in terms of the structure, whatever you can share one level below, how do you structure teams? Is it around outcomes? Is it around features of the product? Is it around type of persona? How do you think about that?
turns.zh: 就结构而言，无论您可以在下面的一级共享什么，您如何构建团队？是围绕结果吗？是围绕产品的功能吗？与角色类型有关吗？您对此有何看法？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. So, we have a core team who's really responsible for the core end to-end user experience. In many ways, they're both doing feature development and then they're also doing growth work. So, they're thinking about how do we build new features and functionalities to help our core personas, which is typically folks who are in sales, recruiting and customer success. So, anyone in an externally facing role, we're really trying to help them do their jobs better. So, the core team's thinking about features and functionalities to really help our core end user persona. And then growth work to think about the PLG funnel, everything from acquisition, activation, conversion, and retention. So, that's one group. (00:17:49): And then, second group is our "enterprise group." And they're really thinking about two different personas. One is the IT admin, the person who needs to make sure that Calendly is secure and that they have all the reporting mechanisms to be able to manage their account and all the tools to manage users and groups at scale. And the second piece of that is also departmental leaders. So as Calendly selling into or being used by a sales organization, the head of sales is not the IT admin, but they are a Teams admin who needs to manage their organization within Calendly. So, the enterprise group really thinks both about the admin, but also sort of the departments and how do we better serve departments. (00:18:31): And then lastly, we have a platform team who's really thinking about how do we embed Calendly into the business processes of the organizations that we support and that we provide our product into. And so, that's everything from partnerships and integrations to our APIs.
turns.zh: 是啊是啊。因此，我们有一个真正负责核心端到端用户体验的核心团队。在很多方面，他们都在进行功能开发，然后也在进行增长工作。因此，他们正在考虑如何构建新的特性和功能来帮助我们的核心角色，这些角色通常是从事销售、招聘和客户成功的人员。因此，对于任何一个面向外部的角色，我们都在努力帮助他们更好地完成工作。因此，核心团队正在思考特性和功能，以真正帮助我们的核心最终用户角色。然后，增长工作要考虑 PLG 漏斗，包括获取、激活、转化和保留等各个方面。所以，这是一组。 (00:17:49)：然后，第二组是我们的“企业组”。他们实际上正在考虑两种不同的角色。一类是 IT 管理员，他们需要确保 Calendly 的安全，并且拥有能够管理其帐户的所有报告机制以及大规模管理用户和组的所有工具。第二部分也是部门领导。因此，当 Calendly 向销售组织进行销售或由销售组织使用时，销售主管不是 IT 管理员，而是需要在 Calendly 中管理其组织的 Teams 管理员。所以，企业集团不仅要考虑管理，还要考虑部门的排序，以及如何更好地为部门服务。 (00:18:31)：最后，我们有一个平台团队，他们真正考虑如何将 Calendly 嵌入到我们支持并提供产品的组织的业务流程中。这就是从合作伙伴关系和集成到我们的 API 的一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So, it's like problem focused/persona focused. Who are you trying to sell it to?
turns.zh: 有趣的。所以，这就像以问题为中心/以角色为中心。你想把它卖给谁？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: That's right, that's right. Yeah, trying to sell it to, and then the persona of who's going to be using the functionality. And then, really having those teams hone and own those personas as they're developing functionality within the product.
turns.zh: 没错，没错。是的，试图将其出售给将要使用该功能的人。然后，真正让这些团队在开发产品功能时磨练并拥有这些角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's your take on OKRs? Do you all use OKRs in some form?
turns.zh: 您对 OKR 有何看法？你们都以某种形式使用 OKR 吗？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yes, we do. We use OKRs both at the company level. So, we have three main OKRs that we're focused on for this year, for example, across the whole company. And then we have department level OKRs, many of which are in support of the company level OKRs, but then there's some additional things that we'll be doing at the department level, for example, that aren't going to show up at the company level. So yeah, we use them both at the company as well as on the product side.
turns.zh: 是的，我们愿意。我们在公司层面使用 OKR。因此，我们今年重点关注整个公司的三个主要 OKR。然后我们有部门级别的 OKR，其中许多都是支持公司级别的 OKR，但是我们将在部门级别做一些额外的事情，例如，这些事情不会出现在公司级别。所以，是的，我们在公司和产品方面都使用它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you've learned about making OKRs work? People love them. People hate them.
turns.zh: 关于让 OKR 发挥作用，您学到了什么吗？人们爱他们。人们讨厌他们。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something you do to make OKRs work? Something you've changed, something you've learned over time in how to work with OKRs?
turns.zh: 您是否采取了一些措施来使 OKR 发挥作用？在如何使用 OKR 方面，您已经改变了一些东西，还是随着时间的推移您学到了一些东西？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah. When I first joined, I'd say we didn't have this muscle well built out. We didn't really have a clear product strategy at the time or clear OKRs guiding the work. And so, there was a lot of great work happening, but it really was unclear how it all fit together or how we were going to measure success in that work. So that was a first phase. I think the second phase for us was we developed a product strategy. We then had product team OKRs that corresponded to that product strategy, but they were really contained to the product team and each department across the organization had their own kind of siloed OKRs. (00:20:20): And then, phase three, where really, I'd say we headed into this year, we have a really clear set, as I mentioned, of company OKRs and then in these really tightly integrated plans across the company around how we're going to support the key results and ultimately deliver on the objectives. And this has been a really incredible transformation of dependency mapping, being able to make sure that we're pulling all the levers across the organization to drive our most important objective. (00:20:47): So, I think it's just the kind of maturing of the business from almost no OKRs to product team OKRs to now company OKRs in a really tight planning process to make sure there's a lot of integration across the company to support what we need to do as a business.
turns.zh: 是的。当我第一次加入时，我想说我们的肌肉还不够发达。我们当时并没有真正明确的产品策略，也没有明确的 OKR 来指导工作。因此，有很多伟大的工作正在发生，但确实不清楚它们如何组合在一起，或者我们如何衡量这项工作的成功。这是第一阶段。我认为我们的第二阶段是制定产品策略。然后，我们制定了与该产品策略相对应的产品团队 OKR，但它们实际上包含在产品团队中，并且组织中的每个部门都有自己的孤立 OKR。 (00:20:20)：然后，第三阶段，实际上，我想说的是，我们进入了今年，正如我提到的，我们有一套非常明确的公司 OKR，然后在整个公司的这些真正紧密整合的计划中，围绕我们将如何支持关键结果并最终实现目标。这是依赖映射的一次真正令人难以置信的转变，能够确保我们在整个组织中调动所有杠杆来推动我们最重要的目标。 (00:20:47)：所以，我认为这只是业务的成熟，从几乎没有 OKR 到产品团队 OKR，再到现在公司 OKR，在一个非常严格的规划过程中，以确保整个公司有大量的整合来支持我们作为一个企业需要做的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, what I'm hearing is one of the biggest changes in learnings was to connect OKRs across from the top to the bottom, right?
turns.zh: 所以，我听到的是学习中最大的变化之一是将 OKR 从上到下连接起来，对吗？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Absolutely. Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对地。绝对地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else that has made a big impact on your ability to build and ship and execute as a company in terms of changes you've made in terms of how the company and how the teams build?
turns.zh: 就您在公司和团队构建方式方面所做的改变而言，是否还有其他事情对您作为一家公司的构建、交付和执行能力产生了重大影响？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: I think one of the biggest changes that we've made, when I first joined, again, we had a product that served a lot of horizontal users. We help solo users who are freelancers, consultants. We help sales teams, we help recruiting teams, we help customer success, we help folks in education. So, we had a very broad user base. And what that means is that product managers in particular are I think had a really hard time prioritizing. At any point in time, it was really difficult to say, should I do work on feature A or for feature B without that clarity? And so, I think one of the most impactful things we did pretty early on in my tenure here was to hone in on our overall product strategy, but a poor piece of that being what's the actual market we're going after? What are the segments of that market? Who are the personas within the segments of that market? (00:22:09): And so, we've made a pretty clear distinction now that while a lot of the feature work that we'll do to support our target personas of sales teams, customer success teams and recruiting teams will impact folks who are not in those personas. Those are the core ICPs that we're going after. And so, historically, that would've been always a sort of trade off decision and a question. And now I think we have a lot of rigor around who our target market and then persona we're going after. And so, teams can use that to prioritize and also just deliver better value for those users.
turns.zh: 我认为我们所做的最大的改变之一是，当我第一次加入时，我们再次拥有了一个为大量横向用户提供服务的产品。我们帮助自由职业者、顾问等独立用户。我们帮助销售团队，我们帮助招聘团队，我们帮助客户成功，我们帮助人们进行教育。所以，我们拥有非常广泛的用户群。这意味着我认为产品经理很难确定优先顺序。在任何时候，如果没有那么清晰，真的很难说，我应该在功能 A 上工作还是在功能 B 上工作？因此，我认为我们在任职初期所做的最有影响力的事情之一就是磨练我们的整体产品策略，但其中一个糟糕的部分是我们要追求的实际市场是什么？该市场有哪些细分市场？该市场细分市场中的角色是谁？ (00:22:09)：因此，我们现在已经做出了非常明确的区分，虽然我们将为支持销售团队、客户成功团队和招聘团队的目标角色所做的许多功能工作将影响那些不属于这些角色的人。这些是我们要追求的核心 ICP。因此，从历史上看，这始终是一种权衡决定和一个问题。现在我认为我们对我们的目标市场和我们要追求的角色有很多严格的要求。因此，团队可以利用它来确定优先级，并为这些用户提供更好的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, it sounds like the biggest unlock and one of the biggest unlocks for making the team more efficient, move faster, make decisions quicker, is narrowing in on exactly who you're going to be selling to.
turns.zh: 因此，这听起来像是最大的解锁，也是让团队更高效、更快行动、更快做出决策的最大解锁之一，就是缩小你的销售对象。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: I think it's one of the harder things for companies to do. So, it sounds relatively easy, and I think most companies believe that they have clarity around this. But then when you go down into the weeds of asking someone who's product manager or a designer, I don't know that it's always as clear because there's always a bit of a hesitation to say no, right? And the idea of saying no is scary. When in reality, the ability to say no is going to allow you to make sure you're building something that's going to be amazing for the people that matter most and not something that's going to be average or okay for a lot of different people.
turns.zh: 我认为这是公司最难做的事情之一。所以，这听起来相对容易，而且我认为大多数公司都认为他们对此很清楚。但是，当你深入询问产品经理或设计师的人时，我不知道它总是那么清楚，因为总是有点犹豫要不要拒绝，对吧？拒绝的想法是可怕的。事实上，拒绝的能力将使你能够确保你正在构建的东西对最重要的人来说是令人惊叹的，而不是对很多不同的人来说平庸或还可以的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was there anything that was really hard about actually executing that, convincing people we're going to narrow and not worry about these people and any lessons from going through that process? Because I imagine a lot of founders listening are like, "Oh, that sounds we should be doing this, but oh man, we're leaving all this money on the table, people are going to be pissed."
turns.zh: 在实际执行过程中，是否有什么真正困难的事情，说服人们我们将缩小范围，而不是担心这些人以及从整个过程中获得的任何教训？因为我想象很多创始人听后都会说，“哦，这听起来我们应该这样做，但是天哪，我们把所有这些钱都留在了桌子上，人们会生气的。”

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's a pretty big cultural shift. So, some of this intersects with the shift from product led growth to adding in a sales motion. So, when I joined Calendly, all of our ARR came from our PLG channel. We didn't have a sales team, we just hired a CRO who was going to build out a sales team. And so, in that world, the way you think about product, the way you think about processes, even the people you have on the team are tailored to that business model. And then, as we sort of moved up market and have now explicitly started to go after teams of users and departments of users and organizations of larger scale, everything about people, process, and product all changes. (00:24:29): I think I touched on culture because I think that's pervasive across the entire organization. The way that things get done has to be highly integrated versus can be a bit more siloed when you're just sort of the self-service PLG business that in many ways runs itself through the product being well optimized. So, there's a lot of process change that needs to happen, the type of people that you need to bring into the organization, that changes as you layer in the new selling motion. And then the product itself of course has to change. (00:24:56): So, I guess let's just say the example of PLG and SLG or the direct selling motion is tied in to your question around what are the things that need to change in order to get clear on your target user? And I think it's highly cultural in nature across people, across process, and then obviously across the actual product itself.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这是一个相当大的文化转变。因此，其中一些与从产品主导增长到增加销售行动的转变相交叉。所以，当我加入 Calendly 时，我们所有的 ARR 都来自我们的 PLG 渠道。我们没有销售团队，只是聘请了一名 CRO，他将组建销售团队。因此，在那个世界中，你思考产品的方式，你思考流程的方式，甚至你团队中的人员都是针对该商业模式量身定制的。然后，当我们进入市场并明确开始追求用户团队、用户部门和更大规模的组织时，有关人员、流程和产品的一切都发生了变化。 (00:24:29)：我想我谈到了文化，因为我认为文化在整个组织中普遍存在。完成工作的方式必须是高度集成的，而当您只是自助式 PLG 业务时，它在很多方面都通过良好优化的产品来运行，而这种方式可能会更加孤立。因此，需要进行大量流程变更，您需要将人员类型带入组织，这些变更会随着您在新销售活动中的分层而变化。那么产品本身当然也必须改变。 (00:24:56)：所以，我想我们只是说 PLG 和 SLG 或直销动议的例子与您的问题有关，为了弄清楚您的目标用户，需要改变哪些事情？我认为它本质上是高度文化的，跨越人、跨越流程，然后显然跨越实际产品本身。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a whole bunch of questions about how Calendly grows and maybe we just get into some of the stuff because I imagine a lot of people are interested. First, let me ask this. I imagine Calendly mostly grows through, I sign up for Calendly, they send it to everyone when I book a meeting and they're like, "Oh, what is this?" And they're like, "Oh, cool, I'm going to use this." And then they start using, it spreads, and then sales eventually finds people at a company that are using it a lot and tries to get the whole company in it. Is that roughly right?
turns.zh: 我对 Calendly 如何发展有一大堆问题，也许我们只是讨论其中的一些内容，因为我想很多人都感兴趣。首先，我想问一下这个问题。我想 Calendly 大部分都会成长，我注册了 Calendly，当我预订会议时他们会将其发送给每个人，他们会说，“哦，这是什么？”他们会说，“哦，太酷了，我要用这个。”然后他们开始使用，它传播开来，然后销售最终找到公司里经常使用它的人，并试图让整个公司都参与其中。大致是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah. Seventy percent of our signups come through that viral loop that you referred to. And then, of those signups, then they're usually solo users and then they start to invite team members in and then the team starts using Calendly and then usually the head of that team either inbounds to us or we have some sort of PQL data to know we should go after that team lead to try and have a conversation around expanding Calendly across their entire organization.
turns.zh: 是的。我们百分之七十的注册来自您提到的病毒循环。然后，在这些注册者中，他们通常是单独用户，然后他们开始邀请团队成员加入，然后团队开始使用 Calendly，然后通常该团队的负责人会联系我们，或者我们有某种 PQL 数据知道我们应该跟踪该团队负责人，尝试围绕在整个组织中扩展 Calendly 进行对话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And PQL, product qualified lead, right?
turns.zh: 还有 PQL，产品合格领先，对吧？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: You got it. Yep.
turns.zh: 你明白了。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, what a loop. What a magical way to grow that everybody wishes they could have.
turns.zh: 哇，真是一个循环。这是一种多么神奇的成长方式，每个人都希望自己能拥有。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: It's pretty incredible, I will say.
turns.zh: 我会说，这真是令人难以置信。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man. Okay, so going back to the question. When did Calendly hire their first salesperson, like any learnings about just how to start down that road once you start a product?
turns.zh: 噢，伙计。好吧，那么回到问题上来。 Calendly 何时雇佣了他们的第一位销售人员，比如在推出产品后如何开始走这条路？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah. As I mentioned, when I joined two years ago, we just hired our first CRO and the PLG business really represented 99% of our ARR. And then, over the last two years, we've scaled the sales team in our SLG motion. Our sales led growth motion now represents about 20% of our ARR and it's actually the fastest growing segment of the business. I think there's probably two things I would touch on in terms of early sales hires. I think the first is, when you're making that transition from PLG to adding in the sales led motion, because you're starting from PLG, it's tends to be much more inbound in nature. You've got these sales reps who are working leads who have usually proactively reached out interested or as we mentioned PQLs. They have data to tell them that this is someone who has usage within their team, and therefore, we should reach out. (00:27:17): And so, that's a very different profile of a sales team member than you might need after you need to pursue more of a heavy outbound motion, more of a hunter profile than a grower profile. So, I think that's the first piece is just make sure you think about the motion when you're moving towards a sales led model. In those early days, it's more inbound in nature, and so the type of sales reps you might need are not necessarily going to be outbound, heavy kind of hunting sales reps.
turns.zh: 是的。正如我提到的，当我两年前加入时，我们刚刚聘请了第一位 CRO，PLG 业务确实占我们 ARR 的 99%。然后，在过去的两年里，我们在 SLG 计划中扩大了销售团队的规模。我们以销售为主导的增长动议现在约占我们 ARR 的 20%，它实际上是业务中增长最快的部分。我认为在早期销售招聘方面我可能会谈到两件事。我认为第一个问题是，当您从 PLG 过渡到添加销售主导动议时，因为您是从 PLG 开始的，所以本质上往往更多是入站式的。这些销售代表是工作领导者，他们通常会主动主动联系感兴趣的人，或者正如我们提到的 PQL。他们有数据告诉他们，这是在他们的团队中使用的人，因此，我们应该联系。 (00:27:17)：因此，在您需要追求更多的外向行动之后，销售团队成员的形象与您可能需要的非常不同，更多的是猎人形象而不是种植者形象。所以，我认为第一件事就是确保你在转向销售主导模式时考虑到这一动议。在早期，本质上更多的是内向销售代表，因此您可能需要的销售代表类型不一定是外向型、重型狩猎销售代表。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just one quick question on that actually, because that's really interesting. I don't know how involved you are in hiring these folks, but is it like, look at their background and they've worked at a company like that? Or is it personality type? Is there anything to look for specifically there?
turns.zh: 实际上只是一个简单的问题，因为这真的很有趣。我不知道你对雇用这些人的参与程度如何，但是看看他们的背景，他们是否在这样的公司工作过？还是性格类型？那里有什么特别需要寻找的吗？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah, I think it is mostly background and the type of selling that they've done previously more so than personality type. But I think the second piece, that's important too, and I'll answer your question on that one too, which is the target buyer. So, when you transition from PLG to sales led or adding this direct sales motion, the buyer is usually just the department head. It's the head of sales, it's the head of rev ops, it's the head of recruiting and it's not a senior person in IT or the CIO. And so, selling into this audience is different than selling into IT. (00:28:32): And so, I think you have to be sure again that you have the right fit of sales folks with the target buyer in those early days. And so, to your question around what's that mean? You wouldn't necessarily want to bring on a bunch of sales folks who are at Oracle who are heavy in selling into CIOs in the early days because that's just not who you're the buyer's going to be. I mean, think we will graduate there eventually, but it's probably going to start from team lead to someone in IT to eventually a CIO led purchase, but that's certainly several years away. And so, making sure that the profile, the folks you're bringing on early match that target buyer in addition to match the motion around how you're going to be acquiring customers.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这主要是背景和他们之前所做的销售类型，而不是性格类型。但我认为第二个问题也很重要，我也会回答你关于第二个问题的问题，即目标买家。因此，当您从 PLG 过渡到销售主导或添加这种直接销售行动时，买家通常只是部门负责人。他是销售主管、运营主管、招聘主管，而不是 IT 或 CIO 的高级人员。因此，向这些受众销售与向 IT 销售不同。 (00:28:32)：所以，我认为您必须再次确保在早期阶段您的销售人员与目标买家是合适的。那么，对于你的问题，这意味着什么？你不一定想聘请一群早期在 Oracle 大量向 CIO 推销产品的销售人员，因为那不是你的买家。我的意思是，我认为我们最终会在那里毕业，但可能会从团队领导开始，到 IT 人员，最终由 CIO 领导的采购，但这肯定还需要几年的时间。因此，请确保您早期引入的个人资料与目标买家相匹配，并且与您将如何获取客户的动态相匹配。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And to see that, is it similar? You look at the companies they worked at, it's like PLG-ish companies.
turns.zh: 看看它是否相似？你看看他们工作过的公司，就像 PLG 式的公司。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Definitely. Yeah, exactly. Yep. Yep.
turns.zh: 确实。是的，完全正确。是的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So, along the same lines, as a product leader working with a strong and large sales team, anything you've learned about just how to build that relationship and build a product org that works really closely and well with a sales org?
turns.zh: 好的。因此，同样，作为与强大而庞大的销售团队合作的产品负责人，您是否学到了如何建立这种关系并建立一个与销售组织真正密切和良好合作的产品组织？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: The first piece that really starts with is customer empathy. And at the end of the day, seeing the sales team and the go-to-market team as this really great asset that can help you as a product manager get closer to the customer. So, I've certainly seen organizations or been in organizations where the product team doesn't necessarily want to be bothered by sales, but I sort of flip that on the head and say sales and sort of the go-to-market teams in general could be your biggest asset to helping you get your job done well. (00:30:07): When I was at Box, I was a product manager on the enterprise team and I spent a ton of time in the field and I don't know how I would possibly know how to have what to have built or how to build it to solve the needs of our customers if I didn't have that close relationship with the sales team and be able to lean on them because they're talking to, 10X of them were customers that I was able to ever talk to within any given week, really lean on them to be the voice of the customer to help me make the best product decisions that I could.
turns.zh: 真正开始的第一个部分是客户同理心。归根结底，将销售团队和市场推广团队视为真正重要的资产，可以帮助您作为产品经理更接近客户。所以，我确实见过或曾经在一些组织中，产品团队不一定希望受到销售的困扰，但我有点翻转这一点，并说销售和一般的市场推广团队可能是帮助你做好工作的最大资产。 (00:30:07)：当我在 Box 时，我是企业团队的产品经理，我在该领域花费了大量时间，如果我没有与销售团队建立密切的关系并且能够依靠他们，因为他们正在与他们交谈，我不知道我怎么可能知道如何构建什么或如何构建它来解决客户的需求，其中 10 倍是我能够在任何给定的一周内与之交谈的客户，真的很精益让他们代表客户的声音，帮助我做出最好的产品决策。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: The core challenge of being a product manager, right?
turns.zh: 成为产品经理的核心挑战，对吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to add that I feel like the core job of PM is just tell people what's next, what's the next thing.
turns.zh: 补充一点，我觉得 PM 的核心工作就是告诉人们接下来会发生什么，接下来会发生什么。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: That's right, and hopefully, you have a good reasoning as to why that thing, next is going to have the biggest impact, which is really where I start. I think it really starts with a clear product strategy that will dictate a few things. And I like this framework that's taken from a book called Playing to Win and it talks about how strategy is really just an integrated set of choices that outline how you're going to win in whatever marketplace you choose. And so, a good product strategy is going to answer questions like, what's your sort of winning aspiration, but maybe more importantly, where are you going to play? What are the markets you're going to go after? What are the segments of those markets? What are the personas in the segments of those markets? And then, how are you going to win with a target audience? (00:32:59): And so, what I think this framework does kind of dovetails back to what I was saying before around prioritization is it forces you to create clarity around where you're going to play and where you're not going to play. And so, this really helps the product team hone in on delivering value for a very clear set of people versus trying to build something for everyone. And so, once you've established what that strategy is or what the playing field you're going to go after, then I think you can divide up your product work and service of that strategy. (00:33:28): So, I'll give you an example. At Calendly, we have the sort of vision, our winning aspiration to become the best place to schedule, prepare for and follow up on your external meetings. And then, we've articulated three horizons around how we're going to get there. Now, the year one that I was here, the percentage of resources we spent on that first horizon and the second horizon was about a 70/30 split and we put 0% of our resources on horizon three. That was too far out in the future and we didn't want to make any investments there quite yet, but we knew where we were going. (00:34:00): In year two, it shifted. We went to a 50/50 split between horizon one and horizon two, but still, no explicit investments in Horizon three. And then, as we're entering to year three now, we've significantly scaled back the investment in horizon one, that's about 30% and then we've got 60% in horizon two and call it 10 in horizon three. So, I think just to close on the question of prioritization, I think it starts with a really clear product strategy which defines where you're going to play and how you're going to win. And then, the work and the percentage of allocation just should feed right into that product strategy and how you're doing against where you need to be in order to achieve ultimately your winning aspiration.
turns.zh: 是的，希望您对为什么接下来的事情会产生最大的影响有一个很好的推理，这确实是我开始的地方。我认为这实际上是从一个明确的产品策略开始的，该策略将决定一些事情。我喜欢这个框架，它取自一本名为《Playing to Win》的书，它讲述了战略实际上只是一组综合的选择，概述了您将如何在您选择的任何市场中获胜。因此，一个好的产品策略将回答这样的问题：你的获胜愿望是什么，但也许更重要的是，你要在哪里玩？您要关注哪些市场？这些市场有哪些细分市场？这些市场细分中的人物角色是什么？然后，你将如何赢得目标受众？ (00:32:59)：所以，我认为这个框架与我之前所说的优先级相吻合，它迫使你明确你将在哪里玩和你不会在哪里玩。因此，这确实有助于产品团队专注于为一组非常明确的人群提供价值，而不是试图为每个人构建一些东西。因此，一旦您确定了该策略是什么或您要追求的竞争环境是什么，那么我认为您可以划分该策略的产品工作和服务。 (00:33:28)：所以，我给你举个例子。在 Calendly，我们有这样的愿景，我们渴望成为安排、准备和跟进外部会议的最佳场所。然后，我们围绕如何实现这一目标阐明了三个愿景。现在，我在这里的第一年，我们在第一个地平线和第二个地平线上花费的资源百分比约为 70/30，而我们将 0% 的资源放在第三个地平线上。那是太遥远的未来，我们还不想在那里进行任何投资，但我们知道我们要去哪里。 (00:34:00)：第二年，情况发生了变化。我们在第一阶段和第二阶段之间进行了 50/50 的分配，但仍然没有对第三阶段进行明确的投资。然后，当我们现在进入第三年时，我们大幅缩减了第一阶段的投资，大约为 30%，然后我们在第二阶段的投资为 60%，并在第三阶段将其称为 10。因此，我认为，为了结束优先级问题，我认为它始于一个非常明确的产品策略，该策略定义了您将在哪里玩以及如何获胜。然后，工作和分配百分比应该直接融入该产品策略以及您如何根据需要达到的目标进行工作，以最终实现您的获胜愿望。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know how much you could share here, but is there a feature that is people keep asking for it and it hasn't been built because of the strategy, the long-term vision, something that's like, "Nope, it doesn't fit. We're not going to do this."
turns.zh: 我不知道你能在这里分享多少，但是有一个功能是人们一直要求的，但由于战略、长期愿景而没有建立，比如“不，它不合适。我们不会这样做。”

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah, I think the best example I can give is there's lots of small businesses and solopreneurs who would love us to have a Venmo integration. We have a PayPal integration. But our target market that we're really trying to go after as our primary persona are as I've mentioned, these sort of core ICPs within organizations. So, sales teams, recruiting teams, customer success teams. And so, it doesn't make sense within those personas to pursue something like a Venmo integration. Now, there's a lot of things we'll build for those personas that are going to help the small business, the solopreneur, the freelancer, but that specific feature is something that would be clearly deprioritized given the current strategy.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为我能给出的最好的例子是，有很多小企业和个体企业家希望我们能够集成 Venmo。我们有 PayPal 集成。但正如我所提到的，我们真正努力追求的目标市场是我们的主要角色，即组织内的这些核心 ICP。所以，销售团队、招聘团队、客户成功团队。因此，在这些角色中追求 Venmo 集成之类的东西是没有意义的。现在，我们将为这些角色构建很多东西来帮助小企业、个体企业家、自由职业者，但考虑到当前的策略，这个特定的功能显然会被降低优先级。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome example. I want to get back to the growth stuff, but before I do that, we're kind of on this topic of planning and a cares and prioritization. I'd love to know just how you do planning at Calendly? How far out do you plan in detail? How far do you have roadmaps? How often do you plan? Anything you can share there?
turns.zh: 这是一个很棒的例子。我想回到增长的话题，但在这之前，我们先讨论一下规划、关心和优先顺序这个话题。我很想知道你们在 Calendly 是如何进行规划的？您具体计划到什么程度？您的路线图还有多远？你多久计划一次？有什么可以分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: This starts again, I sound like a broken record, but with this really clear strategy around where we're going over the next couple of years and then we take that and we break that down into what are the most important things we need to do as a company this year in order to be able to make the right progress against that strategy. So, we have the company level OKRs and I mentioned that we have about three of those this year. And then, those KRs within the company, OKRs are measured annually, but we have milestones across a quarterly basis so we can measure progress more frequently than obviously on the annual or semi-annual basis. (00:36:19): So, I think that's kind of at the high level. And then, obviously our product roadmaps are going to be in support of those key results that we needed to deliver to the business over the course of the year, but then broken down on a quarterly basis. (00:36:30): I think one thing I'll just touch on real fast on is estimations and dates. Something we've done over the last year is really kind of moved to a model of talking about dates and promising and committing to dates that are within our control. And so, if you think about the product development life cycle, we can commit to a discovery effort of doing research around a certain problem space and we can have a general sense of when we know that effort's going to conclude. We don't know if we're going to actually end up going, and based on the results whether we're going to actually move forward with investing in that area, but that's a body of work we can commit to. (00:37:05): From there, we then move into, "Okay, if this is something a problem space we want to go after, we're going to go work on a couple different solutions and we're going to go do some user testing and we're going to land on a solution," and that's another sort of phase we can commit to. Then, once we actually have that completed and we actually know not just the problem but the solution, we can do estimation planning and actually have a date for delivery from an engineering perspective. And so, we've gotten a lot better at making the commitments around the work that's right in front of us versus making a commitment around a project six months out when we haven't even done enough discovery, enough design and ideation to have a real clear understanding of estimation.
turns.zh: 这又开始了，我听起来像是打破了记录，但是有了这个非常明确的战略，围绕着我们未来几年的发展方向，然后我们将其分解为我们作为一家公司今年需要做的最重要的事情，以便能够根据该战略取得正确的进展。因此，我们有公司级别的 OKR，我提到今年我们有大约三个。然后，公司内部的 KR、OKR 每年都会进行衡量，但我们每季度都有里程碑，因此我们可以比每年或半年更频繁地衡量进度。 (00:36:19)：所以，我认为这是较高水平的。然后，显然我们的产品路线图将支持我们在一年中需要向业务交付的那些关键成果，但随后按季度进行细分。 (00:36:30)：我想我要快速谈及的一件事是估算和日期。去年我们所做的事情实际上已经转变为一种讨论日期、承诺并承诺我们控制范围内的日期的模式。因此，如果您考虑产品开发生命周期，我们可以致力于围绕某个问题空间进行研究的发现工作，并且我们可以大致了解该工作何时会结束。我们不知道我们是否会真正结束，也不知道根据结果我们是否会真正推进在该领域的投资，但这是我们可以致力于的工作。 (00:37:05)：从那里开始，我们进入“好吧，如果这是我们想要解决的问题空间，我们将研究几个不同的解决方案，我们将进行一些用户测试，然后我们将找到一个解决方案”，这是我们可以承诺的另一个阶段。然后，一旦我们真正完成了这项工作，并且我们实际上不仅知道问题，还知道解决方案，我们就可以进行估算规划，并从工程角度实际确定交付日期。因此，与我们在六个月后的项目上做出承诺相比，我们在围绕眼前的工作做出承诺方面做得更好，当时我们甚至还没有进行足够的发现、足够的设计和构思来对估算有一个真正清晰的理解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really cool. Do you have terms for these phases, like these phases you have to get through these kinds of gates? Yeah, how do you describe that?
turns.zh: 这真的很酷。您是否有这些阶段的条款，例如您必须通过这些类型的大门的这些阶段？是啊，你怎么形容呢？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah, so the first phase we just call generally discovery. The second phase, we call solutioning. The third phase, build. And then, the fourth phase is launch, measure and iterate.
turns.zh: 是的，所以第一阶段我们通常称之为发现。第二阶段，我们称之为解决。第三阶段，构建。然后，第四阶段是启动、测量和迭代。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 凉爽的。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: And then, we've designed the product development lifecycle around that framework.
turns.zh: 然后，我们围绕该框架设计了产品开发生命周期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, discovery for example, is that a roadmap item for a quarter and that's like what you've committed to? And if that goes well, the next quarter has the next step.
turns.zh: 那么，例如，发现，这是一个季度的路线图项目吗？这就像您所承诺的那样？如果进展顺利，下个季度会有下一步。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. You got it.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。你明白了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Okay. In terms of the strategy artifacts, how does that look or do you have a Google Doc with a template that you all use? What does that look like? What's interesting about people not working at a company or working at just one company is they only have, strategy documents are really hard to see and see examples of. So, I'm always curious what these looks like. So, whatever you can share about what they look like and where you put them and how long and that kind of thing.
turns.zh: 甜的。好的。就策略工件而言，它看起来怎么样？或者你们有一个带有大家都使用的模板的 Google 文档吗？那看起来像什么？对于不在一家公司工作或只在一家公司工作的人来说，有趣的是他们只有战略文件，很难看到和看到例子。所以，我总是很好奇它们是什么样子的。因此，您可以分享有关它们的外观、放置位置以及放置时间等信息。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: We have a couple of different layers of this. I think the first is this high-level three-year strategy and this is actually called at the company level. So, if the doc, it also has slides that have been presented many times to the company when we're in the process of making sure that, that is part of new hire orientation so that everyone should understand where are we going over the next three years and then therefore how does this year's objectives fit into that. So, I think that's at that level. (00:39:07): And then, from there, we've got our product team OKRs. These generally start by docs and we write them in docs. So, they usually get translated into slides at some point for presentation purposes to the company and those are stored centrally in a location and then you get down to the feature level or the project level. And we have different kind of templates for the teams to use based on the type of work that they're going to be doing. And we're a pretty heavy Confluence culture, so we tend to use Confluence as one of the tools for housing and storing information around the work that's being done.
turns.zh: 我们有几个不同的层面。我认为第一个是这个高层三年战略，这实际上是在公司层面上调用的。因此，如果文档中还有幻灯片，当我们确定这一点时，它已经向公司多次展示过，这是新员工入职培训的一部分，以便每个人都应该了解我们未来三年的目标，以及今年的目标如何与之相适应。所以，我认为这就是那个水平。 (00:39:07)：然后，从这里开始，我们就得到了产品团队的 OKR。这些通常以文档开始，我们将它们写在文档中。因此，它们通常会在某个时候被翻译成幻灯片，以便向公司演示，并且这些幻灯片集中存储在某个位置，然后您可以深入到功能级别或项目级别。我们有不同类型的模板供团队根据他们将要做的工作类型使用。我们的 Confluence 文化相当浓厚，因此我们倾向于使用 Confluence 作为围绕正在完成的工作容纳和存储信息的工具之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. So, maybe on that topic, what else is in the stack of Calendly product team tools?
turns.zh: 凉爽的。那么，也许在这个主题上，Calendly 产品团队工具堆栈中还有哪些内容？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: We talked about roadmap planning, some combination of starts with docs, there's mural boards involved. Usually, it ends in slides. Then actually roadmap tracking, we use Aha and we use Airtable collaboration/communication. We use Slack, we use Loom, bug management, we use Jira. I'm trying to think of, is there any other?
turns.zh: 我们讨论了路线图规划、开始与文档的一些组合，以及涉及的壁画板。通常，它以幻灯片结束。然后实际上是路线图跟踪，我们使用 Aha 并使用 Airtable 协作/通信。我们使用 Slack，我们使用 Loom，错误管理，我们使用 Jira。我试着想一想，还有其他的吗？

turns.en: Confluence, you mentioned.
turns.zh: 你提到的融合。

turns.en: Confluence. Yep. Confluence is what we use quite a bit. Pando, we use quite a bit of Pando to help educate users within the product when we're launching new features. Yeah, I think that's the main stack.
turns.zh: 合流。是的。 Confluence 是我们经常使用的。 Pando，当我们推出新功能时，我们使用大量 Pando 来帮助教育用户。是的，我认为这是主要堆栈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And docs is Google Docs and slides is Google Slides.
turns.zh: docs 是 Google Docs，slides 是 Google Slides。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: You got it. Yep.
turns.zh: 你明白了。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet.
turns.zh: 甜的。

turns.en: That's right.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I'm going to bounce around and go back to growth questions and then I have a couple more product team questions. How did Calendly get their first thousand users?
turns.zh: 好的。我将回过头来讨论增长问题，然后我还有几个产品团队问题。 Calendly 是如何获得第一批一千名用户的？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: A great question and I had to fact check it with my CEO earlier this morning, but there's actually a few really interesting things about this story and a few things that Tope did in the early days to get 2,000 users. So, for those who aren't familiar Tope, our CEO and founder started his career in sales and he spent lots of years in sales. And so, he was very used to the challenges of trying to organize external meetings with prospective customers. So, he knew the problem space really, really well. And he had evaluated all the scheduling solutions that were on the market and came to conclusion that there really weren't any great products out there and especially there weren't any great products for the recipient of the actual booking service. And so, I think he saw this as an opportunity for disruption. So, he raided his 401k, he took out all his savings. He didn't make raise any money.
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的问题，今天早上我必须与我的首席执行官核实一下，但实际上这个故事有一些非常有趣的事情，以及 Tope 在早期为获得 2,000 个用户所做的一些事情。因此，对于那些不熟悉托普的人来说，我们的首席执行官兼创始人的职业生涯始于销售，并在销售领域度过了多年。因此，他非常习惯于尝试组织与潜在客户的外部会议的挑战。所以，他非常非常了解问题空间。他评估了市场上的所有调度解决方案，并得出结论，确实没有任何出色的产品，特别是对于实际预订服务的接收者来说，没有任何出色的产品。因此，我认为他认为这是一个颠覆的机会。于是，他搜查了他的401k，拿出了所有积蓄。他没有筹集到任何资金。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a lot of penalties, taking out money at that point.
turns.zh: 那是很多罚款，那时就拿钱了。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Sort of. That's a very good point. I've never asked him about that. And he hired an outside development firm actually in out of the Ukraine to build the first version of Calendly. So, that's the background on Calendly. Why it's important is that the first 10 users were actually customer success agents at a company in the education space that contracted with the same firm that Tope was using to build Calendly. So, he really found his first set of users through the firm that he was using to build the product. (00:41:51): And then, those CSMs or customer success managers were actually using Calendly to schedule calls with parents in K through 12 education. And so, then those parents started using Calendly for their own parent-teacher conference scheduling. And then from there, the school started using it and then all the parents within the school started using it for lots of other use cases and it grew organically from there. So that was one piece. (00:42:17): I think the other piece that's really important is that he started off by just having a free tier. The entire product was free. Some of this came from honestly not being able to actually build the billing infrastructure that would be required to actually charge. So, it came a little bit out of necessity, but it was also free. So not only was it a better product than the alternatives out there, but it was also free. So, the combination of the viral loop and coming in through getting those first 10 users as part of the firm he was using and then the free aspect or I think what led to the first 2,000, and then 10,000, and millions of users from there.
turns.zh: 有点像。这是一个很好的观点。我从来没有问过他这件事。他聘请了一家实际上位于乌克兰的外部开发公司来构建 Calendly 的第一个版本。这就是 Calendly 的背景。之所以重要，是因为前 10 位用户实际上是教育领域一家公司的客户成功代理，该公司与 Tope 用来构建 Calendly 的同一家公司签订了合同。因此，他确实通过他用来构建产品的公司找到了第一批用户。 (00:41:51)：然后，这些 CSM 或客户成功经理实际上使用 Calendly 安排与 K 至 12 教育家长的通话。因此，这些家长开始使用 Calendly 来安排自己的家长会。然后从那里开始，学校开始使用它，然后学校内的所有家长开始将它用于许多其他用例，并且它从那里开始有机增长。所以那是一件。 (00:42:17)：我认为另一件真正重要的事情是他一开始就拥有免费套餐。整个产品是免费的。其中一些原因是实际上无法实际构建实际收费所需的计费基础设施。所以，它的出现有点出于必要，但它也是免费的。因此，它不仅是比现有替代品更好的产品，而且还是免费的。因此，病毒循环和通过让前 10 个用户成为他所使用的公司的一部分而进入，然后是免费方面，或者我认为是什么导致了前 2,000 个，然后是 10,000 个，以及数百万用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is crazy. I have never heard a story like that where the team that is building your product ends up being the source of initial growth.
turns.zh: 那太疯狂了。我从未听说过这样的故事：构建产品的团队最终成为最初增长的源泉。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: I know, pretty crazy.
turns.zh: 我知道，非常疯狂。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God. So many nice things happening in this history of Calendly.
turns.zh: 我的天啊。 Calendly 的历史上发生了很多美好的事情。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: I know.
turns.zh: 我知道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And wow, in Ukraine. So, I'm actually from Ukraine.
turns.zh: 哇，在乌克兰。所以，我实际上来自乌克兰。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Oh nice. That's awesome.
turns.zh: 哦，不错。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's pretty cool.
turns.zh: 太酷了。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah, they're great. [inaudible 00:43:11].
turns.zh: 是的，他们很棒。 [听不清 00:43:11]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and it's also interesting that it's rare that you hear a successful business starts with contractor engineers. I think OICs are like, "Do not do that." So that's a cool counter example of it can actually work out, especially if they're your first users and spread it to others.
turns.zh: 是的，而且有趣的是，你很少听说成功的企业是从承包商工程师开始的。我认为伊斯兰会议组织就像是“不要那样做”。所以这是一个很酷的反例，它实际上可以发挥作用，特别是如果他们是你的第一个用户并将其传播给其他人。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: And we still work with them. They're fantastic and they have incredible engineers, so they're still part of our culture, which is great.
turns.zh: 我们仍然与他们合作。他们非常棒，拥有令人难以置信的工程师，所以他们仍然是我们文化的一部分，这很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, Calendly got big in Ukraine, it sounds like initially.
turns.zh: 所以，Calendly 在乌克兰做大了，听起来像是一开始。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: There you go. There you go.
turns.zh: 就这样吧。就这样吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's something that would surprise people in terms of how Calendly grows today or grew through its history?
turns.zh: Calendly 今天的发展或历史上的发展有哪些事情会让人们感到惊讶？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Most people probably think about Calendly as the scheduling link and really for individual users to reduce the back and forth of email and scheduling. So, they think of that one-on-one use case and I think people would be surprised to learn that our team's business, so multiple users in an organization who want to collaboratively schedule together is growing much faster than our solo user business. And that's really where the future of where we think growth will come from is supporting these teams of users who are in externally facing roles and selling into departments and supporting multi-departmental deployments of Calendly across an entire organization. (00:44:17): So, I think it's still really well known as this solo user tool to eliminate the back and forth of email, but the growth of what we're seeing and where we think it's going to go is actually more teams of users and departments of users and then multiple departments in an organization.
turns.zh: 大多数人可能将 Calendly 视为日程安排链接，真正为个人用户减少电子邮件和日程安排的来回。因此，他们想到了一对一的用例，我认为人们会惊讶地发现我们团队的业务，因此组织中希望一起协作安排的多个用户的增长速度比我们的单独用户业务快得多。这确实是我们认为未来增长的来源，即支持这些面向外部的角色并向部门销售的用户团队，并支持整个组织中 Calendly 的多部门部署。 (00:44:17)：所以，我认为它仍然是众所周知的消除电子邮件来回的独立用户工具，但我们所看到的增长以及我们认为它将走向的实际上是更多的用户团队和用户部门，然后是组织中的多个部门。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting when you hear the story of Calendly that just has so many good things happening, basically for free, it's just grows so well. I think people don't realize you eventually will, that'll slow down, it'll taper off eventually. You'll need to drive growth very actively in these new ways that you're describing. And I think people don't often realize that they just wanted to find something that was viral and then things are going to go great, but it tapers off.
turns.zh: 当你听到 Calendly 的故事时，这很有趣，它发生了很多好事，基本上是免费的，它发展得很好。我认为人们没有意识到你最终会，这会放慢速度，最终会逐渐减弱。您需要以您所描述的这些新方式非常积极地推动增长。我认为人们通常不会意识到他们只是想找到一些病毒式传播的东西，然后事情就会进展顺利，但它会逐渐减弱。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, there's only so many people who, solo users who are going to pull out a credit card. And I think once you also get to hundreds of millions of dollars of revenue scale, just the law of large numbers, it means that growth will slow. And so, you have to figure out where's that next growth curve going to come from. I think the beauty of Calendly is that while we certainly have built features and functionality to support teams and departments, we got pulled there. It wasn't one of those things where we sort of said, "We need to find our next growth lever. Let's go build X." Our customers really pulled us there by the way that they were using the product. (00:45:30): And so again, a very fortunate position to be in, but when you can see in the data and see how customers are using it, that they want to be working on scheduling with their teams, that was our early sign, that's where the business was going to go in the future.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，只有这么多人，单独用户会拿出信用卡。而且我认为一旦你也达到数亿美元的收入规模，仅根据大数定律，就意味着增长将会放缓。因此，你必须弄清楚下一条增长曲线从何而来。我认为 Calendly 的美妙之处在于，虽然我们确实已经构建了支持团队和部门的特性和功能，但我们还是被吸引到了那里。我们并不是说“我们需要找到下一个增长杠杆。让我们去构建 X”。我们的客户确实通过他们使用该产品的方式将我们吸引到了那里。 (00:45:30)：同样，这是一个非常幸运的位置，但是当你可以在数据中看到客户如何使用它时，他们希望与他们的团队一起进行调度，这是我们的早期迹象，这就是未来业务的发展方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't think I mentioned this, I'm paying user of Calendly. It's what I use for booking these podcast episodes.
turns.zh: 我想我没有提到这一点，我是 Calendly 的付费用户。我用它来预订这些播客剧集。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You got me. I think I started when it was totally free and I was like, "How will they ever make money?" This is too much power.
turns.zh: 你抓住了我。我想我是在它完全免费的时候开始的，我当时想，“他们将如何赚钱？”这力量太大了。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: And then, now, you learned that it was free almost by accident.
turns.zh: 然后，现在，您几乎偶然得知它是免费的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yep. I was like, "Yeah, please take my money. This makes my life easier." What are some fun or unique traditions and cultural kind of components of the Calendly product team?
turns.zh: 是的。我当时想，“是的，请拿走我的钱。这让我的生活更轻松。” Calendly 产品团队有哪些有趣或独特的传统和文化组成部分？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: A couple of fun ones I thought we could talk about. One, we have a meeting called OPA, which stands for opportunity/problem, assessment. And so, what this is, it's a meeting where basically PMs, I don't even go to it's a meeting for PMs to really debate and discuss with each other and spar around either areas and problems that they want to go investigate or after they've gotten data back or research back from evaluating an opportunity, deciding whether we actually want to move forward and go try to develop a solution. So, it's really in the product development lifecycle of letting product managers really get into a room with each other on a frequent basis and just think through things, debate, discuss. And I know that they all get a lot of value out of that.
turns.zh: 我想我们可以谈谈一些有趣的事情。第一，我们有一个名为 OPA 的会议，它代表机会/问题、评估。所以，这是什么，这是一个基本上是产品经理的会议，我什至不去参加这个会议，产品经理们可以真正地相互辩论和讨论，围绕他们想要调查的领域和问题进行争论，或者在他们从评估机会中获得数据或研究回来后，决定我们是否真的想继续前进并尝试开发解决方案。因此，在产品开发生命周期中，让产品经理真正经常坐在一起，思考问题、辩论、讨论。我知道他们都从中获得了很多价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of something just like a bad version of that. I had a friend who was a PM at Zynga and he said there's a meeting where PMs present their plans to all the other PM. It was like you're in a shark tank where everyone's coming to destroy you. They just point out all the problems. That's all it ever is in this.
turns.zh: 它让我想起了一些事情，就像它的一个糟糕版本。我有一个朋友，他是 Zynga 的产品经理，他说有一个会议，产品经理们会向所有其他产品经理介绍他们的计划。就像你在一个鲨鱼池里，每个人都会来消灭你。他们只是指出所有的问题。这就是一切。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: I would say on this one, it's the opposite where I feel like everyone really needs the meeting. They're like, "Ugh, I really need to take this to OPA because I need to, I'm working through these problems and I really want to bounce it off of other people." So, I could imagine a world where it would be that. Actually, part of the reason I don't go to the meeting is that I really want everyone to be able to be open and transparent and provide feedback and not feel like there's any judgment from me or any needing to act a certain way because I'm in the room. So, that's sort of why I intentionally don't go. (00:47:44): Another fun one we do is something we call competitive work gaming. So, on some sort of time interval, sometimes it's been quarterly, we'll have assigned people into groups for the quarter to own a competitor. And their job is to essentially spend a lot of time immersing themselves into the product of the competitor, really trying to think through the lens of, do a SWAT analysis, really try to think through the lens of where's this competitor going and how Calendly only think about that and as it relates to our strategy. (00:48:12): And so, we spent a quarter doing that and then we have the competitive war gaming day where every team comes and presents and there's prizes and it's a lot of fun, but it's a really great way to stay on top of what's happening across the market without requiring every product manager designer to be deep in the weeds, there are a lot of different competitors. We can bring all of that knowledge together through what we call competitive work gaming.
turns.zh: 我想说的是，在这一点上，情况恰恰相反，我觉得每个人都真正需要这次会议。他们会说，“呃，我真的需要把这个问题提交给 OPA，因为我需要这样做，我正在解决这些问题，我真的很想向其他人反馈。”所以，我可以想象一个这样的世界。事实上，我不去参加会议的部分原因是我真的希望每个人都能够公开透明并提供反馈，而不是因为我在房间里而觉得我有任何判断或需要以某种方式采取行动。所以，这就是我故意不去的原因。 (00:47:44)：我们做的另一件有趣的事情是我们称之为竞争性工作游戏。因此，在某种时间间隔内，有时是季度，我们会在该季度将人员分组以拥有竞争对手。他们的工作本质上是花大量时间让自己沉浸在竞争对手的产品中，真正尝试从这个角度思考，进行 SWAT 分析，真正尝试从这个竞争对手的走向以及 Calendly 如何只考虑这一点以及它与我们的战略相关的角度思考。 (00:48:12)：所以，我们花了四分之一的时间来做这件事，然后我们进行了竞争性的战争游戏日，每个团队都来展示，都有奖品，这很有趣，但这是一个非常好的方法，可以了解整个市场正在发生的事情，而不需要每个产品经理设计师都深入了解，因为有很多不同的竞争对手。我们可以通过所谓的竞争性工作游戏将所有这些知识整合在一起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is cool. It's really impressive how you do these exercises and they seem really positive and friendly and constructive. It sounds like there is a pretty unique culture at Calendly. I'm curious if there's anything else that's core to the values or the way that you think about the principles of building product at Calendly.
turns.zh: 那很酷。你做这些练习的方式真的令人印象深刻，它们看起来非常积极、友好和建设性。听起来 Calendly 有一种非常独特的文化。我很好奇是否还有其他核心价值观或您对 Calendly 构建产品原则的思考方式。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: What I touched on earlier is really core to how we build product, which is honing in on this target user and honing in on our target market. I do think it's quite rare. I think in most organizations that I've seen, I think there's a desire to do that. But I think, again, when it push comes to shove, it's really hard for executives to make decisions that say no to things. One of Calendly's actually core principles is focus wisely. It's pretty deeply embedded into our culture. And so, I think one of the reasons that I've been successful in being able to create the clarity around who the target personas are is because I think it's embedded into the culture of Calendly to focus wisely. (00:49:29): So, I don't know that it'll work in every organization. I think many organizations really struggle to say no, and they're always adding more onto the plate versus taking off. But I do think from an ethos perspective, there is something around focusing and the ability to focus to therefore deliver the highest quality of product that you can to your target customers. That is unique and I think it starts with some of the broader cultural paradigms that exist at the company and then we've now embedded that into the way we think about how we build product.
turns.zh: 我之前谈到的是我们如何构建产品的真正核心，即针对目标用户和目标市场进行磨练。我确实认为这是非常罕见的。我认为在我见过的大多数组织中，我认为都有这样做的愿望。但我再次认为，当事情到了紧要关头时，高管们真的很难做出拒绝的决定。 Calendly 实际上的核心原则之一是明智地聚焦。它已经深深地融入了我们的文化中。因此，我认为我能够成功地明确目标人物角色的原因之一是因为我认为明智地聚焦已融入到 Calendly 的文化中。 (00:49:29)：所以，我不知道它是否适用于每个组织。我认为许多组织确实很难拒绝，而且他们总是在增加更多的东西而不是起飞。但我确实认为，从精神的角度来看，有一些围绕专注和专注的能力，从而为目标客户提供最高质量的产品。这是独一无二的，我认为它始于公司存在的一些更广泛的文化范式，然后我们现在将其嵌入到我们思考如何构建产品的方式中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else you do to instill that? It sounds like it's a core value. Do you put posters around the office? So how else do you keep people focused?
turns.zh: 你还做其他什么事情来灌输这一点吗？听起来这是一个核心价值。你在办公室周围张贴海报吗？那么，你还能如何让人们集中注意力呢？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: We're a fully remote company. So, now you've got my brain going on. Are there some sort of virtual sticky notes that you could get people to put onto their laptops to remind them?
turns.zh: 我们是一家完全远程的公司。所以，现在你已经让我的大脑运转起来了。是否有某种虚拟便签可以让人们贴在笔记本电脑上以提醒他们？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Backgrounds to show us [inaudible 00:50:16].
turns.zh: 向我们展示的背景 [听不清 00:50:16]。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Yeah, it's embedded into a lot of the documentation. So, it's embedded into the templates that I talked about in terms of, everything from sort of the way we structure that OPA, document that folks are going to be working on and debating too when they go to create the actual sort of PRD. When teams come in to present as part of our product reviews, we have a template that keeps reinforcing who's the target customer, who's the target user within that customer base, what are their needs and then how are we going to solve their needs better than any alternative that there is on the market. So, I think there's lots of different reinforcing mechanisms to that focus.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。是的，它已嵌入到很多文档中。因此，它嵌入到我谈到的模板中，从我们构建 OPA 的方式到人们在创建实际类型的 PRD 时将要处理和讨论的文档，一切都包括在内。当团队作为我们产品评论的一部分进行展示时，我们有一个模板，不断强调谁是目标客户，谁是该客户群中的目标用户，他们的需求是什么，然后我们将如何比市场上的任何替代方案更好地解决他们的需求。因此，我认为有很多不同的强化机制可以强化这一重点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like sometimes things like that come from a big problem the company had and then you index weigh the other side, focus, here's the four people we all build for. It becomes instilled in the culture.
turns.zh: 我觉得有时这样的事情来自公司遇到的一个大问题，然后你索引权衡另一面，重点，这是我们为之打造的四个人。它被灌输到文化中。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: And I think you're right. I mean, because Calendly started as such a horizontal product, which was amazing because that's how it grew so virally and so it had the entry, the wedge into scheduling and how our first horizon and becoming the best horizontal scheduling automation platform was because we had that horizontal focus. And so, it was a blessing. But as we think about transitioning to horizon two, which is really about deepening our support for these teams and departmental users as well as verticals, that's I think the inflection point where we said, in order to shift us from horizon one to horizon two, we need to be making some real trade off decisions and we need to create this focus so that we can actually allow teams to go do that. (00:51:52): So, I think it's a really good point. We sort of had to create clarity around focus because we were trying to make a shift from broad horizontal platform serving lots of users to a deeper investment into specific users and specific teams of users within departments.
turns.zh: 我认为你是对的。我的意思是，因为 Calendly 最初是一个横向产品，这很神奇，因为它如此迅速地发展，因此它进入了调度领域，并成为了最好的横向调度自动化平台，因为我们有横向关注点。所以，这是一种祝福。但当我们考虑过渡到地平线二时，这实际上是为了加深我们对这些团队和部门用户以及垂直领域的支持，我认为这就是我们所说的拐点，为了将我们从地平线一转向地平线二，我们需要做出一些真正的权衡决策，我们需要创建这个焦点，以便我们实际上可以允许团队这样做。 (00:51:52)：所以，我认为这是一个非常好的观点。我们必须明确重点，因为我们试图从服务大量用户的广泛横向平台转向对部门内特定用户和特定用户团队进行更深入的投资。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before Calendly, you were at Box. Before that, you were at Glassdoor. I'm going to ask two different questions. You could pick which direction you want to go. What would you say are the biggest differences culturally between these three? If you had to bucket, here's how I'd describe Glassdoor, Box, Calendly. Or what did you take from those two places that you bring with you to Calendly and future opportunities?
turns.zh: 在 Calendly 之前，您在 Box。在此之前，您在 Glassdoor。我要问两个不同的问题。你可以选择你想去的方向。您认为这三者之间最大的文化差异是什么？如果你非要说的话，我会这样描述 Glassdoor、Box、Calendly。或者你从这两个地方给 Calendly 带来了什么以及未来的机会？

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: I love this question. So, they're all different, which is why I just feel so fortunate to have had experiences that were all quite different. So, starting with Box, maybe I'll take your second question. Box, when I joined, we were in the process of moving up market and trying to capture as much enterprise market share as possible, and I was on the enterprise product management team. So, I spent a lot of time, as I mentioned earlier, talking to customers. And in my first year in particular trying to ramp on the business. And I'd say my biggest learning during that time was around how to ask the right questions to really understand the why behind what a customer was asking for and then figuring out how to build a solution to their problem that would also meet the needs of a broader swath of customers. (00:53:07): It became very clear early to me if I would just go build what customer A wanted and what customer B wanted and the customer C wanted, not only would that be wasted effort to do it three times, but more importantly, what they wanted me to go build was going to have a negative impact on the end user experience. And preserving that end user experience was so critical. So, learning how to ask the right questions to understand the actual problem and then build the solution that's going to be most scalable to that problem set across lots of customers was probably my biggest learning from Box. (00:53:37): Moving to Glassdoor, totally different business model. Glassdoor is actually really more of a consumer business and 60 million unique users go to Glassdoor every month and it's a marketplace between job seekers and employers and it's highly, highly dependent on the consumer engagement, growing traffic, getting that traffic to come and engage and apply to jobs. And so, during my time as CPO there, I was responsible now for both sides of that marketplace, the consumer business and the B2B. And so, I learned all about how do you build PR consumer products, how do you think about optimization of a funnel? How do you think about building up a growth team and growth as a discipline? How do you use data and AB testing to make decisions? (00:54:17): So, I think that kind of consumer mentality and how you approach product, I then have brought with me to Calendly, which is really a blend of both, right? Calendly is first, as we've talked about a PLG business and it looks a lot more like a consumer business like Glassdoor. And then, it's got this direct selling business that looks a lot more like Box's enterprise business. So, I think I've been able to take kind of lessons learned from both Box and Glassdoor and apply them together to Calendly.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个问题。所以，它们都是不同的，这就是为什么我感到很幸运能够拥有完全不同的经历。那么，从 Box 开始，也许我会回答你的第二个问题。 Box，当我加入时，我们正在向高端市场迈进，并试图占领尽可能多的企业市场份额，而我是企业产品管理团队的成员。因此，正如我之前提到的，我花了很多时间与客户交谈。尤其是在我的第一年，我特别努力扩大业务。我想说，那段时间我最大的学习就是如何提出正确的问题，以真正理解客户要求背后的原因，然后找出如何为他们的问题构建一个解决方案，同时满足更广泛客户的需求。 (00:53:07)：我很早就很清楚，如果我只是去构建客户 A 想要的、客户 B 想要的和客户 C 想要的，不仅会浪费三次精力，而且更重要的是，他们希望我构建的东西会对最终用户体验产生负面影响。保持最终用户体验非常重要。因此，学习如何提出正确的问题来理解实际问题，然后构建最适合大量客户的问题集的解决方案可能是我从 Box 学到的最大的东西。 (00:53:37)：转向 Glassdoor，完全不同的商业模式。 Glassdoor 实际上更像是一个消费者业务，每月有 6000 万独立用户访问 Glassdoor，它是求职者和雇主之间的市场，它高度依赖于消费者的参与度、不断增长的流量、吸引流量来参与并申请工作。因此，在担任 CPO 期间，我现在负责该市场的双方：消费者业务和 B2B。因此，我了解了如何构建公关消费产品，您如何看待渠道优化？您如何看待建立增长团队以及将增长作为一门学科？您如何使用数据和 AB 测试来做出决策？ (00:54:17)：所以，我认为这种消费者心态以及对待产品的方式，我后来带到了 Calendly，这确实是两者的融合，对吧？ Calendly 是第一个，因为我们已经讨论过 PLG 业务，它看起来更像 Glassdoor 这样的消费者业务。然后，它的直销业务看起来更像 Box 的企业业务。因此，我认为我已经能够从 Box 和 Glassdoor 中吸取经验教训，并将它们一起应用到 Calendly 中。

turns.zh: 和招聘。是啊是啊。不寻找任何新东西。好的。最后一个问题。你是 Skip 社区的一部分，我相信 Nikhyl 和一些人管理着这个社区。因此，我很想听听有关此内容的一些信息，以及如果人们适合的话如何加入。

turns.speaker: Annie Pearl
turns.en: Yeah, as you mentioned about two years ago, Nikhyl, who was the former CPO of Credit Karma and is now a VP of product at Meta, got a small group of CPOs together who were all going through similar phases of companies' growth, late stage growth companies, and we all were facing the same challenges in our roles. And he formalized this community as a way to help us gather advice from one another, talk through how to manage challenges we're facing and just make us more successful in the roles. And we always joke, we're like the support group. (00:55:37): We meet on Sundays and it has been incredibly valuable as I've sort of gone through the last couple of years in my role at Calendly. Since then, we've grown the group to about 23 heads of products and CPOs and expanded the charter a bit, which I think is interesting to help product leaders not just be successful in their current role, but also how to think about setting them up for success in the role after this. (00:55:59): And so, we're experimenting with a couple of different interesting ways to help product leaders grow. One of them is we're actually partnering with some companies right now to experiment with how can we help them as they're looking to make their first head of product hire or their first C O hire really hone in on what they're looking for and partnering with the talent partners we know to really help try to increase the success that they find the right candidates. That's something interesting we're doing. (00:56:23): We also recently launched a podcast covering some topics like, how do you manage the next job search, how do you avoid burnout, breaking down things like equity, and other kind of timely topics. And then also, we just have an active Discord server where we've got all sorts of channels from topics, how to manage the CEO/CPO partnership, compensation, even sharing planning, even sharing some advising opportunities or other CPO roles that kind of come across our radar. (00:56:53): So, it's been a really, really cool kind of experiment to see how the power of the community. And I know Lenny, you do a ton of stuff around community, how that has helped all of us. I think it's just more effective in our roles and feel like we have a group of people who are behind us supporting us during what is a very hard role.
turns.zh: 是的，正如您大约两年前提到的那样，Nikhyl 是 Credit Karma 的前 CPO，现在是 Meta 的产品副总裁，他召集了一小群 CPO，他们都经历过类似的公司成长阶段、后期成长公司，我们都在自己的角色中面临着同样的挑战。他将这个社区正式化，作为一种帮助我们互相收集建议、讨论如何应对我们面临的挑战并让我们在岗位上取得更大成功的方式。我们总是开玩笑，我们就像支持小组。 (00:55:37)：我们每周日见面，这非常有价值，因为我在 Calendly 的角色中经历了过去几年的经历。从那时起，我们的团队已发展到大约 23 名产品负责人和首席产品官，并稍微扩大了章程，我认为这很有趣，不仅可以帮助产品负责人在当前的职位上取得成功，而且还可以考虑如何帮助他们为今后的职位取得成功做好准备。 (00:55:59)：因此，我们正在尝试几种不同的有趣方法来帮助产品领导者成长。其中之一是，我们现在实际上正在与一些公司合作，尝试我们如何帮助他们，因为他们正在寻求让他们的第一位产品负责人或他们的第一位首席首席官招聘真正磨练他们正在寻找的东西，并与我们知道的人才合作伙伴合作，真正帮助他们增加找到合适候选人的成功率。这是我们正在做的有趣的事情。 (00:56:23)：我们最近还推出了一个播客，涵盖一些主题，例如，如何管理下一次求职、如何避免倦怠、分解股权等问题以及其他及时的主题。此外，我们还拥有一个活跃的 Discord 服务器，其中包含各种主题的渠道，包括如何管理 CEO/CPO 合作伙伴关系、薪酬，甚至共享计划，甚至共享一些我们关注的建议机会或其他 CPO 角色。 (00:56:53)：所以，这是一个非常非常酷的实验，旨在了解社区的力量。我知道莱尼，你在社区做了很多事情，这对我们所有人都有帮助。我认为这对我们的角色来说更加有效，并且感觉我们有一群人在我们身后支持我们，度过了一个非常艰难的角色。

turns.zh: 我喜欢这个。我想当人们看到 CPO 时，他们会想象他们已经知道了一切。他们有一群朋友扮演同一个角色，但我认为实际上，很多时候这是一个孤独的角色。因此，我可以看到这样的东西的力量，只是为了帮助人们了解谁适合这个，他们如何找到它，是的，就像 [听不清 00:57:33]。

turns.zh: 那太棒了。我需要那个。我发现我需要阻止日期和更改时间，我只是喜欢在我的日历上、在我的 Calendly 中执行此操作。
